stem: Best guess: a taxpayer's spouse died in October 2025. What filing status can she use for 2025?

choices.explanation: She's considered married for the year of death.
That status applies to the two following years.
Correct. A surviving spouse may file jointly for the year of death.
Not in the year of death, if she's treated as married.

explanation: A surviving spouse may file jointly for the year of death.

stem: Nate is unmarried and pays more than half the cost of his dependent mother's apartment; she lives alone. What filing status may Nate use?

choices.explanation: A dependent parent needn't live with the taxpayer.
Nate isn't married.
Nate isn't a surviving spouse.
Correct. HOH exception: a dependent parent may live in a separate home the taxpayer maintains.

explanation: HOH exception: a dependent parent may live in a separate home the taxpayer maintains.

stem: The 2025 standard deduction for a single filer is $15,750, and the additional amount for age 65 or older is $2,000. A single taxpayer who is 67 and not blind claims the standard deduction for 2025. What is the amount (excluding the separate senior deduction)?

choices.explanation: Omits the additional amount for age.
Uses the married additional amount.
That's the joint amount.

explanation: 2025 single standard deduction 15,750 + 2,000 additional for age 65+ = 17,750.
reviewNote: Uses a One Big Beautiful Bill Act (P.L. 119-21) amount for 2025. Verify against current IRS guidance and exam materials.

stem: Which person can be a qualifying child of the taxpayer?

choices.text: The taxpayer's 25-year-old son, a full-time student, not disabled
choices.explanation: Over the age limit.
Over the age limit and not disabled.

choices.text: The taxpayer's 17-year-old niece who lived with the taxpayer all year and didn't support herself
choices.explanation: Correct. Niece is a descendant of a sibling.

choices.text: A 10-year-old neighbor who lived with the taxpayer for 3 months
choices.explanation: Fails relationship and residency.

explanation: Qualifying child tests: relationship (including descendants of siblings), age, residency, support, and joint return.

stem: Four siblings support their father: A 40%, B 30%, C 20%, D 10%. Under a multiple support agreement, who may claim the father?

choices.explanation: Any sibling providing more than 10% may claim him if the others agree.

choices.text: No one — no one provided over half
choices.explanation: A multiple support agreement solves this.
D doesn't exceed 10%.

choices.text: A, B, or C (by agreement), but not D
choices.explanation: Correct. D provided only 10%, not more than 10%.

explanation: The group must provide more than half; the claimant must provide more than 10%.

stem: A married couple lived apart for the entire second half of 2025. The wife paid all costs of the home where her dependent daughter lived all year. What is the wife's best filing status?

choices.explanation: Correct. Abandoned-spouse rule: considered unmarried if living apart the last 6 months and maintaining a home for a dependent child.
She qualifies as considered unmarried.
She's still married, but considered unmarried for HOH purposes only.
Her spouse is alive.

explanation: Abandoned-spouse rule: considered unmarried if living apart the last 6 months and maintaining a home for a dependent child.

stem: A widower's wife died in 2023. He hasn't remarried and maintains a home for his dependent son. What status may he use for 2025?

choices.explanation: Only for the year of death.
QSS is available and better.
Correct. 2025 is the second year after the year of death.
Better statuses are available.

explanation: QSS applies for the 2 years following the year of death (2024 and 2025 here).

stem: For 2025 the qualifying-relative gross income limit is $5,200. The taxpayer's widowed mother has $4,800 of taxable interest and $12,000 of Social Security benefits, none of which is taxable. Does she meet the gross income test?

choices.explanation: Correct. Gross income counts only taxable income; nontaxable Social Security is excluded.
Nontaxable Social Security benefits are not gross income.

choices.text: No; benefits always count as income
choices.explanation: Only the taxable portion of Social Security counts.

choices.text: Yes; parents have no income test
choices.explanation: The gross income test applies to every qualifying relative, including parents.

explanation: The qualifying-relative gross income test uses taxable gross income; the dollar limit is given on the exam.

stem: For 2025 a dependent's standard deduction is the greater of $1,350 or earned income plus $450 (not more than $15,750). A 16-year-old dependent has $3,000 of wages and no other income in 2025. What is her standard deduction?

choices.explanation: Earned income + $450 is greater.
Omits the $450 add-on.
Limited as a dependent.
Correct. Greater of $1,350 or $3,000 + $450.

explanation: Dependent's standard deduction = greater of $1,350 or earned income + $450 (not above the regular amount).

stem: As of what date is marital status generally determined for filing purposes?

choices.explanation: Status isn't set at the start of the year.

choices.text: December 31 (the last day of the tax year)
choices.explanation: Correct. Marital status is determined at the end of the tax year (or at death).

choices.text: The date the return is filed
choices.explanation: The filing date doesn't matter.
Mid-year isn't the test.

explanation: Marital status is determined at the end of the tax year (or at death).

stem: The 2025 standard deduction for joint filers is $31,500, and the additional amount is $1,600 per spouse age 65 or older. A married couple, both 66, files jointly for 2025. Neither is blind. What is their standard deduction (excluding the separate senior deduction)?

choices.explanation: Omits the additional amounts.
Uses the unmarried additional amount.
Adds only one additional amount.

reviewNote: Uses a One Big Beautiful Bill Act (P.L. 119-21) amount for 2025. Verify against current IRS guidance and exam materials.

stem: Which test does **not** apply to a qualifying child?

choices.explanation: This test applies.
Correct. The gross income limit applies to qualifying relatives.
This test applies.
This test applies.

explanation: Qualifying children have no gross income limit.

choices.explanation: That's the qualifying relative gross income limit.
Correct. Personal exemptions have been permanently eliminated.
The pre-2018 amount.
No exemptions remain.

explanation: The TCJA reduced exemptions to $0, and the One Big Beautiful Bill Act made that permanent.

stem: Tom, a cash-basis taxpayer, died on June 30, 2025. His employer paid his final $8,000 paycheck to his estate in July. His widow has not remarried. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: The $8,000 is IRD taxed to the estate
choices.explanation: Correct. Wages earned but unpaid at death are income in respect of a decedent, reported by the recipient (the estate).

choices.text: The $8,000 goes on Tom's final return
choices.explanation: A cash-basis decedent's final return includes only income received before death.

choices.text: The widow cannot file a joint return
choices.explanation: A surviving spouse who has not remarried may file jointly for the year of death.

choices.text: The standard deduction is cut in half
choices.explanation: The standard deduction on a final return is not prorated.

explanation: IRD is taxed to whoever receives it; the final return covers income through the date of death.

stem: An unmarried parent pays all costs of the home where her 10-year-old son lived all year. What is her best filing status?

choices.explanation: Correct. She has a qualifying child in her home.
HOH gives better rates.
She isn't widowed.
She isn't married.

explanation: An unmarried taxpayer who pays more than half the cost of a home for a qualifying person who lives there over half the year qualifies as head of household.

stem: A taxpayer's 22-year-old daughter is a full-time student who lives at home. Can she meet the qualifying-child age test?

choices.explanation: The student rule extends the limit.

choices.text: Yes, she's under 24 and a student
choices.explanation: Correct. The age limit is 24 for full-time students.
Being a student suffices.

choices.text: Only if she earns no income
choices.explanation: Income isn't part of the age test.

explanation: A qualifying child must be under 19, under 24 if a full-time student, or permanently and totally disabled.

stem: An unrelated friend lived with the taxpayer all year as a member of the household, had $3,000 of gross income, and was fully supported by the taxpayer. Can the friend be a dependent?

choices.explanation: Household members can qualify.
She doesn't meet that test.
Correct. A household member can qualify.

choices.text: Only with a multiple support agreement
choices.explanation: The taxpayer provided all support.

explanation: A person who lives with the taxpayer all year as a household member can be a qualifying relative if the income and support tests are met.

stem: Divorced parents don't sign a release. Their child lived with the mother for 7 months and the father for 5. Who may claim the child as a qualifying child?

choices.explanation: He had fewer months.
That is a tiebreaker for equal time.
The custodial parent has the right.
Correct. The custodial parent, with more nights.

explanation: Absent a release, the custodial parent (with whom the child lived longer) claims the child.
